newsitem.title: UNITED NATIONS: U.N. council renews deadlocked W. Sahara operation.
newsitem.headline: U.N. council renews deadlocked W. Sahara operation.

text.p: The Security Council unanimously approved on Wednesday a six-month renewal of a U.N. operation in Western Sahara where a referendum on whether the territory should incorporate into Morocco or become independent has been repeatedly postponed.

The territory vote originally was scheduled for January 1992. But Morocco, which controls most of the former Spanish colony, and the Polisario Front, which has been battling for independence, disagreed on who should be eligible to take part. Voter identification was halted a year ago.

In accordance with a May Security Council resolution, the U.N. Mission for the Referendum in Western Sahara (MINURSO) has been reduced from a strength of 288 military observers to 230 and from 91 police to nine, while civilian staff has been cut from 410 to 170.

Wednesday's council resolution extending the operation until May 31 asked Secretary-General Boutros Boutros-Ghali, in his next report, to propose "alternative steps, in the framework of the (U.N.) settlement plan, should there be no meaningful progress towards removing the obstacles to the implementation of the plan."
Boutros-Ghali was requested to continue his efforts with the parties to break the impasse and to submit an interim report by Feb. 28.

The resolution, adopted without any speeches, also welcomed "the steps taken by the parties to demonstrate good will, including the release of prisoners, and the recent indications that the parties are moving forward in their efforts to resolve oustanding questions."

This was an allusion to Morocco's release of 66 Sahrawi prisoners -- Polisario last year freed 185 Moroccan prisoners -- and to recent reports of the first private meetings for several years between representatives of both sides.
Morocco's King Hassan said earlier this month talks had been held in Morocco with Polisario but had been inconclusive.

The council reiterated its "commitment to the holding, as soon as possible, of a free, fair and impartial referendum for the self-determination of the people of Western Sahara," in accordance with the long-delayed U.N. plan.

United States U.N. ambassador Madeleine Albright said in a statement she continued to believe a just and equitable solution was possible "but only if both sides demonstrate greater flexibility in exploring realistic compromises and developing greater mutual confidence."

"We cannot continue our efforts indefinitely without more practical results, particularly in light of the mounting cost of a peacekeeping operation which to date exceeds one-quarter of a billion dollars," she said.

"I want to make clear that, unless there is significant progress in reaching a political settlement, the United States could not support a further renewal of MINURSO in its present form," Albright added.

The United Nations announced earlier this month that Major-General Jorge Barrosa de Moura of Portugal would take over command of MINURSO's military contingent on Sunday, succeeeding fellow countryman Major-General Jose Eduardo Garcia Leandro.
